passages.title: Assessing the threat of marine debris
content: For several years, Mira Solvang, a marine ecologist at the Institute for Coastal Research in Bergen, has been turning over a gloomy question: is the state of our ocean rubbish merely grim, or a good deal worse?

Solvang sits on a panel of researchers called the Ocean Litter Assessment Group, whose remit takes in, among other topics, the worsening problem of marine debris — the drifting and sunken waste most people simply call ocean rubbish. Study upon study has rung alarm bells over the state of the seas, and in a recent article in the journal Coastal Science Letters, Solvang and her fellow authors set out to establish how many of these supposed hazards genuinely stand up.

One thing she has noticed repeatedly is that a study will wrap up by guessing at the larger implications of its results. Research may show, say, that a certain fish is swallowing floating scraps of plastic, then warn that the species as a whole could be sliding toward extinction. 'The problem was that these assumed risks had never really been checked,' Solvang says. 'We simply didn't have much to go on.'

Her group worked through more than 130 pieces of research on the consequences of marine debris, all published before the close of 2015. For each, they asked two things: which hazards its authors had examined — 428 supposed hazards in all — and what the evidence had in fact shown.

In about four out of every five instances, the feared consequences of marine litter proved real enough. In the rest, the group found that shortcomings in how the studies had been designed and conducted undermined their conclusions — a missing control group here, unsound statistics there.

Tellingly, just one carefully built study failed to turn up the effect its authors had been looking for — an inquiry into whether oysters came to harm after taking in microscopic particles. The plastic, the scientists observed, passed from the oysters' stomachs into their bloodstream and lingered for weeks; the shellfish, though, seemed none the worse for it.
Oysters, in other words, may take rubbish in their stride; even so, the review painted a far clearer picture of the many kinds of trouble marine debris really does cause.

Among the threats the analysis confirmed, most could be laid at the door of plastic rather than materials such as wood or metal. And it was mainly the more sizeable fragments that did the damage — animals ending up entangled in castoff material, or eating it and injuring themselves badly.

A large share of marine debris, though, is 'microplastic' — fragments no bigger than five millimetres across. Some starts out as an ingredient in cosmetics and toiletries, some as fibres loosened from synthetic garments in the wash, some as the eroded remains of larger objects. Against the many studies of full-sized debris, Solvang's team found little work on how these tiny particles behave. 'With microplastic, many questions remain open,' she says, noting that more has appeared since 2015, when the group closed its survey.

The paths by which debris ends up killing sea creatures are likewise full of unknowns, she adds. Much of the research has fixed on a lone animal — or even its tissues and cells — rather than on entire populations. On top of that, the plastic levels used in laboratory experiments are frequently far higher than anything the ocean itself holds. So nobody can put a figure on how many fish, turtles or seabirds plastic pollution might kill, or say how the loss of one species would tell on the predators above it and on the wider ecosystem.

'We have to start asking questions that carry more ecological weight,' Solvang maintains. More often than not, scientists have no idea how a catastrophe — say, a tanker spilling its whole cargo of oil across a vast stretch of sea — will affect the environment until the event is already behind them. 'We leave the important questions too late,' she says. Yet if researchers can grasp the way marine litter eats away at ecosystems little by little, they may still stop matters from worsening.

Framing the questions well also helps governments, and the public, decide where their attention belongs. The threats that grab the most notice are not always the real priorities. The very name 'Great Pacific Garbage Patch' — a mass of debris in the northern Pacific — tends to summon up some huge floating island of trash. The reality is far less dramatic: much of the waste sits beneath the surface or is too small to see, and a boat could cross the whole area without a single piece coming into view. A Norwegian outfit called Blue Current is now planning to sink machinery into the Patch and similar spots to vacuum up plastic. A recent paper, though, ran simulations suggesting that placing the same devices nearer the coast would curb pollution far more over the long run.

'Putting a few of these misconceptions right really does count,' Solvang says. Whether in the media or within the scientific community, she remarks, 'all those images of stranded and tangled-up animals convince people that plastic is killing off everything in the ocean.' A patient reading of the research already out there helps ecologists tell the problems that truly call for action from those they would do better — as with the oysters — to take in and let pass.

questions.prompt: Solvang was involved in founding the Ocean Litter Assessment Group.

explanation.step1: Solvang was involved in founding the Ocean Litter Assessment Group . Cần kiểm tra Solvang có tham gia thành lập nhóm hay không, chứ không chỉ có thuộc nhóm hay không.
explanation.step2: Dựa vào tên riêng “Ocean Litter Assessment Group” => ta tìm đến câu đầu đoạn 2 để đọc về mối liên hệ giữa Solvang và nhóm. Đoạn 2 — Ocean Litter Assessment Group
explanation.step3: Đoạn 2: Solvang sits on a panel of researchers called the Ocean Litter Assessment Group , whose remit takes in, among other topics, the worsening problem of marine debris — the drifting and sunken waste most people simply call ocean rubbish .
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: Solvang tham gia thành lập nhóm (“ involved in founding ”). Bài đọc nói: Solvang thuộc nhóm (“sits on a panel”), nhưng không cho biết bà có tham gia thành lập nhóm hay không . Đáp án đúng: NOT GIVEN Đối chiếu paraphrasing: involved in founding không có trong bài. Đáp án TRUE Nếu skim/scan thấy Solvang thuộc nhóm (“sits on a panel”), sẽ dễ chọn TRUE Nhưng thuộc nhóm không chứng minh bà tham gia thành lập nhóm. Chỉ chọn TRUE nếu bài xác nhận bà tham gia thành lập nhóm. FALSE Sai vì bài cũng không nói Solvang không tham gia thành lập nhóm. Chỉ chọn FALSE nếu bài phủ nhận vai trò thành lập của bà.

questions.prompt: Fish are more vulnerable to marine litter than any other sea creature.

explanation.step1: Fish are more vulnerable to marine litter than any other sea creature . Cần kiểm tra phép so sánh này, không chỉ tìm chỗ bài đọc nhắc đến cá.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc nhanh đến chỗ bàn về rác biển ảnh hưởng đến cá và các sinh vật khác. Ở đoạn 10, cụm “fish, turtles or seabirds” => đây là điểm bắt đầu cần đọc kĩ. Đoạn 10 — fish, turtles or seabirds
explanation.step3: Đoạn 10: So nobody can put a figure on how many fish, turtles or seabirds plastic pollution might kill , or say how the loss of one species would tell on the predators above it and on the wider ecosystem .
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: cá dễ bị rác biển gây hại hơn mọi sinh vật biển khác (“ more vulnerable to marine litter than any other sea creature ”). Bài đọc nói: chưa ai có thể đưa ra con số cá, rùa hoặc chim biển có thể chết vì ô nhiễm nhựa (“nobody can put a figure on”). Bài không xếp hạng mức độ dễ bị hại của các loài. Không xác định được số con có thể chết không chứng minh cũng không bác bỏ phép so sánh trong câu hỏi. Đáp án đúng: NOT GIVEN Đối chiếu paraphrasing: more vulnerable to marine litter than any other sea creature không có trong bài. Đáp án TRUE Nếu skim/scan thấy đoạn 3 nhắc đến cá nuốt nhựa (“a certain fish is swallowing”), sẽ dễ chọn TRUE Nhưng đoạn đó không so sánh cá với mọi sinh vật biển khác. Chỉ chọn TRUE nếu bài khẳng định cá dễ bị rác biển gây hại hơn tất cả các sinh vật biển khác. FALSE Thấy bài nói chưa thể đưa ra con số (“nobody can put a figure on”), ta có thể tưởng phép so sánh đã bị bác bỏ Nhưng chưa xác định được số lượng không có nghĩa cá không dễ bị hại nhất. Chỉ chọn FALSE nếu bài khẳng định một sinh vật biển khác dễ bị rác biển gây hại hơn cá.

questions.prompt: Solvang's review leaves no doubt that whole populations of fish will soon vanish.

explanation.step1: Solvang's review leaves no doubt that whole populations of fish will soon vanish . Cần kiểm tra cả mức độ chắc chắn lẫn dự đoán về toàn bộ quần thể cá .
explanation.step2: Tên riêng Solvang giúp ta theo các nhận xét của bà. Khi gặp ý nghiên cứu ở cấp cả quần thể (“entire populations”) tại câu 2 đoạn 10, ta bắt đầu đọc kĩ. Đoạn 10 — entire populations
explanation.step3: Đoạn 10: Much of the research has fixed on a lone animal — or even its tissues and cells — rather than on entire populations . So nobody can put a figure on how many fish , turtles or seabirds plastic pollution might kill , or say how the loss of one species would tell on the predators above it and on the wider ecosystem . Câu (2): phần lớn nghiên cứu xét một cá thể thay vì cả quần thể . Câu (4): vì vậy, chưa thể xác định ô nhiễm nhựa có thể giết chết bao nhiêu cá.
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: bản tổng quan khẳng định chắc chắn (“leaves no doubt”) rằng toàn bộ quần thể cá sẽ sớm biến mất. Bài đọc nói: phần lớn nghiên cứu không xét cả quần thể (“rather than on entire populations”), và không ai có thể xác định số cá có thể chết (“nobody can put a figure on how many fish”). Như vậy, mức chắc chắn mà câu hỏi gán cho bản tổng quan trái với giới hạn bằng chứng bài đọc nêu ra . Đáp án đúng: FALSE Đối chiếu paraphrasing: leaves no doubt nobody can put a figure on whole populations of fish a lone animal + rather than on entire populations Đáp án TRUE Nếu skim/scan thấy đoạn 3 nhắc nguy cơ tiến tới tuyệt chủng (“sliding toward extinction”), sẽ dễ chọn TRUE Nhưng đó là điều một nghiên cứu cảnh báo, không phải kết luận chắc chắn của bản tổng quan. Chỉ chọn TRUE nếu bài xác nhận cả quần thể cá sẽ sớm biến mất. NOT GIVEN đáp án này vì bài không nêu thời điểm cá biến mất. Nhưng bài có nói rõ chưa thể xác định số cá có thể chết, nên bác bỏ mức chắc chắn trong câu hỏi. Chỉ chọn NOT GIVEN nếu bài không cho biết liệu bản tổng quan có đủ cơ sở để khẳng định điều đó hay không.

questions.prompt: The group recorded which particular dangers each study had investigated.

explanation.step1: The group recorded which particular dangers each study had investigated . Ý câu hỏi: Nhóm ghi nhận mối nguy mà từng nghiên cứu đã xem xét .
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta tìm chỗ bài nói về việc nhóm rà soát các nghiên cứu. Cụm “Her group worked through” ở đoạn 4 là điểm bắt đầu đọc kĩ. Đoạn 4 — Her group worked through
explanation.step3: Đoạn 4: Her group worked through more than 130 pieces of research on the consequences of marine debris, all published before the close of 2015 . For each, they asked two things: which hazards its authors had examined — 428 supposed hazards in all — and what the evidence had in fact shown . Câu (1): nhóm rà soát các công trình nghiên cứu. Câu (2): với từng công trình , nhóm kiểm tra mối nguy mà tác giả đã xem xét .
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: Nhóm ghi nhận mối nguy cụ thể mà từng nghiên cứu đã xem xét. Bài đọc nói: Với từng công trình (“ For each ”), nhóm kiểm tra tác giả đã xem xét mối nguy nào (“which hazards its authors had examined”). Trong ngữ cảnh rà soát nghiên cứu, đây là thông tin nhóm xác định cho từng công trình. ⇒ Hai ý phù hợp . Đáp án đúng: TRUE Đối chiếu paraphrasing: each study For each particular dangers hazards had investigated had examined FALSE Nếu chỉ thấy bài dùng “asked” thay vì “recorded”, sẽ dễ nghĩ hai ý trái nhau Nhưng bài không phủ nhận việc nhóm xác định mối nguy trong từng công trình. Chỉ chọn FALSE nếu bài nói nhóm không xác định những mối nguy đó. NOT GIVEN Nếu chỉ tìm đúng từ “recorded” mà không thấy, sẽ dễ chọn NOT GIVEN Nhưng “For each” và “which hazards its authors had examined” đã nêu trực tiếp việc nhóm kiểm tra thông tin ấy ở từng công trình. Chỉ chọn NOT GIVEN nếu bài không cho biết nhóm có kiểm tra mối nguy mà từng công trình xem xét hay không.

questions.prompt: In most of the studies examined, the design and methods were reliable.

explanation.step1: In most of the studies examined, the design and methods were reliable . Cần kiểm tra: thiếu sót trong thiết kế và phương pháp xảy ra ở phần lớn hay chỉ ở một phần nhỏ các trường hợp được đánh giá?
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc nhanh đến khi gặp một tỷ lệ tương ứng với ý phần lớn (“most”). Cụm “four out of every five instances” ở đoạn 5 là điểm bắt đầu đọc kỹ. Đoạn 5 — most
explanation.step3: Đoạn 5: In about four out of every five instances, the feared consequences of marine litter proved real enough . In the rest, the group found that shortcomings in how the studies had been designed and conducted undermined their conclusions — a missing control group here, unsound statistics there . Câu (1): khoảng bốn trong năm trường hợp cho thấy hậu quả được lo ngại là có thật. Câu (2): phần còn lại mới là nơi thiếu sót trong thiết kế và cách tiến hành làm suy yếu kết luận . Những thiếu sót ấy được đặt ở phần còn lại, không phải phía đa số .
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: Thiết kế và phương pháp của phần lớn nghiên cứu được xem xét là đáng tin cậy (“most”; “were reliable”). Bài đọc nói: Thiếu sót về cách thiết kế và tiến hành nghiên cứu làm suy yếu kết luận nằm ở phần còn lại (“In the rest”). Vì vậy, nhận định phù hợp với sự đối chiếu trong bài. Đáp án đúng: TRUE Đối chiếu paraphrasing: most about four out of every five instances — bài nêu tỷ lệ theo trường hợp, không đếm chính xác số nghiên cứu. the design and methods how the studies had been designed and conducted were reliable shortcomings; các thiếu sót chỉ được nêu ở In the rest. FALSE Nếu skim/scan thấy “shortcomings”, sẽ dễ nghĩ thiết kế và phương pháp không đáng tin cậy Nhưng cụm “In the rest” giới hạn các thiếu sót ở phần còn lại. Chỉ chọn FALSE nếu bài nói phần lớn nghiên cứu có thiếu sót làm suy yếu kết luận. NOT GIVEN Nếu tìm đúng từ “reliable” mà không thấy, sẽ dễ chọn NOT GIVEN Nhưng hai câu đã cho biết phía nào có thiếu sót và phía nào chiếm đa số. Chỉ chọn NOT GIVEN nếu bài không cho biết các thiếu sót thuộc phần lớn hay phần còn lại.

questions.prompt: The oyster investigation had anticipated that the particles would prove harmful.

explanation.step1: The oyster investigation had anticipated that the particles would prove harmful . Ý câu hỏi: Cần kiểm tra nghiên cứu đã dự đoán điều gì , không phải cuối cùng đã tìm thấy điều gì.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc nhanh đến khi gặp thông tin về hàu và khả năng bị hại (“oysters came to harm”). Cụm này xuất hiện ở đoạn 6 => bắt đầu đọc kỹ tại đây. Đoạn 6 — oysters came to harm
explanation.step3: Đoạn 6: Tellingly, just one carefully built study failed to turn up the effect its authors had been looking for — an inquiry into whether oysters came to harm after taking in microscopic particles .
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: Cuộc điều tra đã dự đoán các hạt sẽ gây hại (“would prove harmful”). Bài đọc nói: Các tác giả trông đợi tìm thấy một tác động (“the effect its authors had been looking for ”); cuộc điều tra xem hàu có bị hại sau khi hấp thụ các hạt hay không (“whether oysters came to harm after taking in microscopic particles”). Nghiên cứu không tìm thấy tác động ấy (“failed to turn up”), nhưng đó là kết quả thực tế, không phải điều họ trông đợi. ⇒ Hai ý thống nhất về dự đoán . Đáp án đúng: TRUE Đối chiếu paraphrasing: had anticipated had been looking for would prove harmful came to harm FALSE Nếu skim/scan thấy nghiên cứu không tìm thấy tác động (“failed to turn up”), sẽ dễ chọn FALSE Nhưng đó là kết quả, không phủ định điều các tác giả đã dự đoán. Chỉ chọn FALSE nếu bài nói họ đã dự đoán các hạt không gây hại. NOT GIVEN Nếu chỉ thấy từ “whether”, sẽ dễ nghĩ bài chỉ nêu câu hỏi nghiên cứu Nhưng “had been looking for” cho biết các tác giả trông đợi tìm thấy tác động. Chỉ chọn NOT GIVEN nếu bài không cho biết họ trông đợi kết quả gì.

questions.prompt: The study found that the particles caused significant harm to the oysters' health.

explanation.step1: The study found that the particles caused significant harm to the oysters' health . Ý câu hỏi: Nghiên cứu có thực sự phát hiện các hạt gây hại đáng kể cho hàu không? Cần kiểm tra kết quả về sức khỏe của hàu , không chỉ xem các hạt có đi vào cơ thể chúng hay không.
explanation.step2: Dựa vào đối tượng cụ thể là hàu (“oysters”) => ta bắt đầu đọc ở câu (1), đoạn 6, nơi nghiên cứu đặt câu hỏi liệu hàu có bị hại (“whether oysters came to harm”). Đoạn 6 — whether oysters came to harm
explanation.step3: Đoạn 6: Tellingly, just one carefully built study failed to turn up the effect its authors had been looking for — an inquiry into whether oysters came to harm after taking in microscopic particles . The plastic , the scientists observed, passed from the oysters' stomachs into their bloodstream and lingered for weeks ; the shellfish , though , seemed none the worse for it . Câu (1): nghiên cứu kiểm tra tác hại của các hạt đối với hàu nhưng không tìm thấy tác hại được dự đoán . Câu (2): nhựa đi vào cơ thể hàu, tuy nhiên hàu dường như không bị hại .
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: Nghiên cứu phát hiện các hạt gây tổn hại đáng kể cho sức khỏe hàu (“caused significant harm”). Bài đọc nói: Nghiên cứu không tìm thấy tác hại được dự đoán (“failed to turn up”); hàu dường như không bị hại (“seemed none the worse for it”). => Hai ý trái ngược nhau. Đáp án đúng: FALSE Đối chiếu paraphrasing: caused significant harm seemed none the worse for it Đáp án TRUE Nếu skim/scan thấy nhựa đi vào máu (“into their bloodstream”), sẽ dễ suy ra hàu bị hại Nhưng kết quả lại nói hàu dường như không bị hại. Chỉ chọn TRUE nếu bài nói các hạt thực sự gây tổn hại đáng kể cho hàu. NOT GIVEN Nếu chỉ đọc việc nhựa đi vào cơ thể, sẽ dễ nghĩ bài không cho biết tác động lên sức khỏe Nhưng câu (2) đã nêu tình trạng của hàu. Chỉ chọn NOT GIVEN nếu bài không cho biết hàu có bị hại hay không.

questions.prompt:
The most serious threats identified were:
• plastic (rather than metal or wood)
• pieces of debris that were _____ (these harm animals)

explanation.step1: - pieces of debris that were 8. ___ (these harm animals) Chỗ trống đứng sau “were”, nên cần một tính từ mô tả những mảnh rác gây hại cho động vật. Chưa thể biết chính xác đặc điểm đó là gì nếu chỉ đọc ghi chú.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khóa đặc biệt; ta tìm cách diễn đạt tương đương với các mảnh rác (“pieces of debris”). Ở đoạn 8, từ “fragments” là điểm bắt đầu đọc. Đoạn 8 — fragments
explanation.step3: Đoạn 8: And it was mainly the more sizeable fragments that did the damage — animals ending up entangled in castoff material , or eating it and injuring themselves badly .
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: sizeable Câu hoàn chỉnh: • pieces of debris that were sizeable (these harm animals) (Những mảnh rác có kích thước lớn ; chúng gây hại cho động vật.) => Khớp với dự đoán về một tính từ mô tả mảnh rác gây hại; đáp án là 1 từ nguyên văn trong bài. Đối chiếu paraphrasing: pieces of debris fragments these harm animals did the damage + animals ending up entangled plastic — nhựa: Từ này đã nằm ở ý ghi chú phía trên và chỉ chất liệu, không phải tính từ mô tả các mảnh rác ở ô số 8. microplastic — vi nhựa: Nếu skim/scan đoạn 9 sẽ dễ chọn vì thấy từ này Nhưng câu (2) đoạn 8 nói chính những mảnh lớn hơn (“more sizeable fragments”) gây hại.

questions.prompt: Few studies had examined _____, for example the kind that comes from synthetic fabrics.

explanation.step1: Few studies had examined 9. ___ , for example the kind that comes from synthetic fabrics . Ô trống cần một danh từ chỉ loại rác hoặc hạt được nghiên cứu. Ví dụ về vải tổng hợp giúp nhận diện loại đó; “Few studies” cho biết phải tìm thông tin về việc có ít nghiên cứu .
explanation.step2: Dựa vào từ khoá khó thay thế là synthetic => bắt đầu đọc ở câu 3 đoạn 9, nơi nhắc đến quần áo tổng hợp (“synthetic garments”). Đoạn 9 — synthetic garments
explanation.step3: Đoạn 9: A large share of marine debris , though, is ' microplastic ' — fragments no bigger than five millimetres across . Some starts out as an ingredient in cosmetics and toiletries, some as fibres loosened from synthetic garments in the wash, some as the eroded remains of larger objects . Against the many studies of full-sized debris, Solvang's team found little work on how these tiny particles behave . Câu (1)–(3): nêu microplastic và ví dụ sợi từ quần áo tổng hợp . Câu (4): nhóm Solvang thấy ít nghiên cứu về những hạt nhỏ này.
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: microplastic Câu hoàn chỉnh: Few studies had examined microplastic , for example the kind that comes from synthetic fabrics. (Ít nghiên cứu đã xem xét microplastic , chẳng hạn loại bắt nguồn từ vải tổng hợp.) => Khớp với dự đoán về một loại rác có thể bắt nguồn từ vải tổng hợp và thông tin “ít nghiên cứu” trong bài; đáp án gồm 1 từ. Đối chiếu paraphrasing: Few studies had examined found little work on comes from synthetic fabrics fibres loosened from synthetic garments fibres “ — sợi vải ”: Đây là ví dụ về nguồn hình thành microplastic, không phải tên đối tượng mà nhóm Solvang nói là có ít nghiên cứu. full-sized debris “ — rác kích thước lớn ”: Câu (4) nói có nhiều nghiên cứu về loại này; nhận định “ít nghiên cứu” dành cho những hạt nhỏ.

questions.prompt:
Weaknesses of the studies examined
• most looked at single animals instead of whole _____
• the _____ of plastic in laboratory work often differed from those found at sea
• too little was known about
– the number of animals that might be affected
– the effect that a drop in one species' numbers would have on its _____
– the effect on the ecosystem

explanation.step1: - most looked at single animals instead of whole 10. ___ Ô trống đứng sau “whole”, nên cần một danh từ chỉ tập thể để đối chiếu với từng con vật riêng lẻ. Dự đoán từ cần điền có thể ở dạng số nhiều.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc đến chỗ bài nói về việc nghiên cứu tập trung vào một con vật riêng lẻ (“a lone animal”) => đây là điểm bắt đầu đọc bằng chứng. Đoạn 10 — a lone animal
explanation.step3: Đoạn 10: Much of the research has fixed on a lone animal — or even its tissues and cells — rather than on entire populations . Hai phía của “rather than” khớp với “single animals instead of whole 10. ___” trong đề. Từ cần điền là đối tượng ở phía sau phép đối chiếu.
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: populations Câu hoàn chỉnh: most looked at single animals instead of whole populations (phần lớn các nghiên cứu xem xét từng con vật thay vì cả quần thể ). => Khớp với dự đoán về danh từ chỉ tập thể và đúng từ trong bài; đáp án gồm 1 từ, đề không nêu giới hạn từ. Đối chiếu paraphrasing: single animals a lone animal instead of whole rather than on entire animal — con vật: Đây là đối tượng nghiên cứu đã tập trung vào, không phải đối tượng cần điền sau “instead of whole”. tissues / cells — mô / tế bào: Đây là thông tin chen giữa về phạm vi nghiên cứu còn hẹp hơn một con vật; không phải một tập thể được đối chiếu với từng con vật.

questions.prompt: Solvang says more needs to be learned about the probable effects of a future _____ — one that releases oil, for instance.

explanation.step1: - the 11. ___ of plastic in laboratory work often differed from those found at sea Ô trống cần một danh từ số nhiều : *those* ở vế sau chỉ lại đại lượng cần điền . Dự đoán đó là từ chỉ mức nhựa được so sánh giữa thí nghiệm và biển.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc nhanh đến khi gặp ý tương đương với việc nghiên cứu nhựa trong phòng thí nghiệm (“laboratory experiments”) ở đoạn 10 => đây là vùng liên quan. Đoạn 10 — laboratory experiments
explanation.step3: Đoạn 10: On top of that, the plastic levels used in laboratory experiments are frequently far higher than anything the ocean itself holds .
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: levels Câu hoàn chỉnh: the levels of plastic in laboratory work often differed from those found at sea (Mức nhựa trong thí nghiệm thường khác mức được ghi nhận ngoài biển.) => Khớp dự đoán về danh từ số nhiều chỉ mức nhựa : bài đọc dùng chính từ levels ; đáp án gồm 1 từ, còn đề cung cấp không nêu giới hạn số từ. Đối chiếu paraphrasing: in laboratory work used in laboratory experiments often differed from those found at sea frequently far higher than anything the ocean itself holds higher — cao hơn: Dễ chọn vì bài đọc so sánh hai môi trường (“far higher”) Nhưng higher là tính từ; ô trống cần danh từ số nhiều. experiments — các thí nghiệm: Từ này xuất hiện trong “laboratory experiments”, nhưng chỉ bối cảnh nghiên cứu, không phải mức nhựa được so sánh. populations — các quần thể: Câu 2 đoạn 10 có “entire populations”, nhưng đó là quần thể động vật, không phải đại lượng của nhựa.

questions.prompt: Complete blank for Question 38:

explanation.step1: – the effect that a drop in one species' numbers would have on its 12. ___ Sau “its” cần một danh từ chỉ đối tượng chịu ảnh hưởng khi số lượng của một loài giảm. Chỉ dựa vào ngữ pháp thì chưa xác định được đó là danh từ số ít hay số nhiều.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta tìm ý tương đương với sự suy giảm số lượng của một loài (“a drop in one species' numbers”). Ở đoạn 10, cụm một loài bị mất đi (“the loss of one species”) cho thấy đây là vùng liên quan. Đoạn 10 — the loss of one species
explanation.step3: Đoạn 10: So nobody can put a figure on how many fish, turtles or seabirds plastic pollution might kill, or say how the loss of one species would tell on the predators above it and on the wider ecosystem .
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: predators Câu hoàn chỉnh: – the effect that a drop in one species' numbers would have on its predators (tác động mà sự suy giảm số lượng của một loài sẽ gây ra cho các loài săn mồi của nó ) => Khớp với dự đoán về nhóm sinh vật chịu ảnh hưởng; đáp án gồm 1 từ. Đề được cung cấp không ghi giới hạn số từ. questions.prompt: Which of the following would make the best heading for the passage as a whole?
options: A fresh solution to the marine debris crisis
Assessing the threat of marine debris
The case for global action on marine debris
questions.correct: Assessing the threat of marine debris

explanation.step1: Which of the following would make the best heading for the passage as a whole ? Câu hỏi hỏi: Nhan đề nào phản ánh đúng nhất toàn bộ bài đọc , thay vì chỉ một ví dụ hay một giải pháp riêng lẻ?
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt để tìm một chi tiết đơn lẻ. Ta bắt đầu ở đoạn 2, nơi tác giả đặt vấn đề liệu những nguy cơ được cảnh báo có thực sự có căn cứ (“supposed hazards genuinely stand up”). Đoạn 2 — supposed hazards genuinely stand up
explanation.step3: Đoạn 2: Study upon study has rung alarm bells over the state of the seas , and in a recent article in the journal Coastal Science Letters, Solvang and her fellow authors set out to establish how many of these supposed hazards genuinely stand up . Đoạn 4: Her group worked through more than 130 pieces of research on the consequences of marine debris , all published before the close of 2015 . Đoạn 5: In about four out of every five instances, the feared consequences of marine litter proved real enough . In the rest, the group found that shortcomings in how the studies had been designed and conducted undermined their conclusions — a missing control group here, unsound statistics there . Đoạn 9: 'With microplastic, many questions remain open ,' she says , noting that more has appeared since 2015, when the group closed its survey . Đoạn 12: The threats that grab the most notice are not always the real priorities . Đoạn 13: A patient reading of the research already out there helps ecologists tell the problems that truly call for action from those they would do better — as with the oysters — to take in and let pass . Câu (2): Câu (2), đoạn 2: đặt câu hỏi liệu các cảnh báo về nguy cơ có đứng vững khi kiểm chứng . Câu (1): Câu (1), đoạn 4: nhóm của Solvang rà soát nghiên cứu về tác hại của rác biển . Câu (1): Câu (1)–(2), đoạn 5: phần lớn tác hại có thật , nhưng một số kết luận bị thiếu sót nghiên cứu làm suy yếu. Câu (4): Câu (4), đoạn 9: vẫn còn điều chưa được giải đáp về vi nhựa. Câu (2): Câu (2), đoạn 12: điều gây chú ý không phải lúc nào cũng đáng ưu tiên. Câu (3): Câu (3), đoạn 13: đọc kỹ bằng chứng giúp phân biệt vấn đề thực sự cần hành động với vấn đề có thể cho qua. Xuyên suốt bài là việc đánh giá các nguy cơ từ rác biển dựa trên bằng chứng, kể cả những điều còn chưa chắc chắn.
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: C. Assessing the threat of marine debris (Đánh giá mối đe dọa từ rác biển). Đối chiếu paraphrasing: Assessing the threat establish how many of these supposed hazards genuinely stand up marine debris giữ nguyên Đáp án A “ Một giải pháp mới cho cuộc khủng hoảng rác biển ”: Đoạn 12 có đề xuất đặt thiết bị gần bờ (“placing the same devices nearer the coast”), nên dễ chọn nhan đề về giải pháp Nhưng đó chỉ là một ví dụ về lựa chọn ưu tiên, không phải trọng tâm toàn bài. Đáp án B “ Rác biển: xác định bên chịu trách nhiệm ”: Đoạn 8 dùng cụm “laid at the door of plastic”, dễ gợi ý ý quy trách nhiệm Nhưng câu ấy xác định vật liệu gây nhiều tác hại, không bàn về bên nào phải chịu trách nhiệm. Đáp án D “ Lập luận kêu gọi hành động toàn cầu về rác biển ”: Đoạn 12 nhắc đến “governments, and the public”, nhưng bài tập trung đánh giá bằng chứng và xác định nguy cơ cần ưu tiên, không xây dựng lời kêu gọi hành động toàn cầu.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part 1. You will hear a visitor reporting a theft to a police officer. First, you have some time to look at questions one to four. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to four.
[00:55] OFFICER: Good morning. How can I help?
[00:57] LOUISE: I need to report a theft. Several things were taken from my bag yesterday.
[01:02] OFFICER: I'm sorry about that. I'll have to record some details first. Could you tell me your name?
[01:11] LOUISE: Louise Taylor.
[01:12] OFFICER: Thank you. Do you normally live in the UK?
[01:16] LOUISE: No, I'm Canadian, although my mother was British.
[01:20] OFFICER: What's your date of birth?
[01:22] LOUISE: The 14th of December, 1977.
[01:26] OFFICER: So you're here on a visit?
[01:27] LOUISE: Yes. I travel over most summers for work. I'm an interior designer and I come to look for antique furniture to buy. The best pieces are often in the smaller towns.
[01:41] LOUISE: The trip had gone very well this year, right up to yesterday.
[01:46] OFFICER: You've been in the country for some time then?
[01:49] LOUISE: Yes, for two months. I'm flying home next week.
[01:53] OFFICER: Where are you staying at the moment?
[01:55] LOUISE: I'm now at Park Apartments on King Street. Before that, I was at Riverside Apartments, also on King Street. But that place was only available for six weeks, so I had to move.
[02:09] OFFICER: And what number is your apartment?
[02:12] LOUISE: Number 15.
[02:13] OFFICER: Right.
[02:16] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions four to ten. Now listen and answer questions four to ten.
[03:01] OFFICER: Now I'll take the details of what happened. You said things were removed from your bag?
[03:06] LOUISE: That's correct.
[03:08] OFFICER: Were you carrying the bag when the theft happened?
[03:11] LOUISE: Yes, which is why I can't make sense of it. I had the backpack on my shoulders. I went into a supermarket for a few items, and when I opened the bag, my wallet had disappeared.
[03:27] OFFICER: What was inside the wallet?

[03:29] LOUISE: Luckily, not my credit cards. I keep those with my passport in an inner section of the backpack. But the wallet held quite a lot of cash, roughly £250. I'd taken £300 out of my account yesterday and had already spent about 50 on shopping.
[03:51] OFFICER: I see.

[03:53] LOUISE: At first I assumed I'd left the wallet in the apartment. Then I noticed my phone was missing too. I'd only bought it a week ago, and that was when I knew someone had stolen from me. At least the keys to my rental car were still there.
[04:11] OFFICER: You said this happened yesterday?
[04:14] LOUISE: Yes.
[04:15] OFFICER: That would make the date the 10th of September. Do you have any idea where and when the items may have been taken?

[04:22] LOUISE: It was hard to work out because the bag stayed on my back from the time I left the apartment after lunch. It's a small backpack, and I use it while travelling because it feels safer than carrying a handbag. I met a friend, and we spent a couple of hours in the museum. When we came out, at about 4 o'clock, several young boys rushed over and crowded around us.
[04:49] LOUISE: They kept asking what time it was, and then they suddenly ran away.
[04:54] OFFICER: Do you remember what any of them looked like?
[04:58] LOUISE: The boy who did most of the talking had a t-shirt with a picture on it. Let me think. It was a tiger.
[05:06] OFFICER: About how old was he?
[05:07] LOUISE: Around 12, I'd say.
[05:09] OFFICER: Can you recall anything else about his appearance?
[05:13] LOUISE: Not a great deal. He was fairly slim.
[05:17] OFFICER: What colour was his hair?
[05:18] LOUISE: That I do remember. He was blonde, whereas all the other boys had dark hair.
[05:25] OFFICER: Anything else about the group?
[05:27] LOUISE: No, not really. Everything happened so fast.
[05:31] OFFICER: Alright. I'll give you a crime reference number to use when you contact your insurer. It contains 10 digits. 87954-82361.
[05:45] LOUISE: Thank you. So should I...

passages.title: Induction Talk For New Apprentices
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Induction Talk For New Apprentices"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a human resources manager giving an induction talk to a group of new apprentices. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Good morning, everyone.

[00:55] AUDIO: I'm Janet Parker, the human resources manager, and I'd like to welcome you to the company. We're delighted that you've joined our apprenticeship program, and I hope the next six months will be both useful and enjoyable. I'll begin with some general guidance about settling in as an apprentice. For most of you, this will be your first experience of working in a large organization, so the opening week may feel rather demanding.

[01:25] AUDIO: You'll be given a great deal of information, but there's no need to memorize all of it immediately. What matters is checking whenever you're uncertain. Your supervisor is easy to approach and will be happy to explain a procedure or point you in the right direction. You're here to learn, so take full advantage of that support.

[01:48] AUDIO: During that first week, you'll work in several different departments, make a point of introducing yourself and speaking to as many members of staff as you can about what they do. Besides learning how the organization fits together, you'll pick up useful information and start building relationships with the people around you. In addition to your supervisor, each of you will have a mentor. This will be someone who finished an apprenticeship fairly recently, and you'll meet once a week.

[02:22] AUDIO: The mentor is there to support you throughout the program, though that certainly doesn't mean doing difficult jobs on your behalf. Instead, they'll help you review the targets you've met, recognize anything that still needs attention, and think through your longer-term career aims. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

[03:32] AUDIO: I'd now like to go over several company rules that apply to apprentices. I'll start with internet use. Some of your duties involve online research, so you can use the internet freely for work. However, it mustn't be used for private browsing.

[03:49] AUDIO: You should use your own phone for anything personal. A number of you have asked about flexible working. Once you've completed the three-month probation period, it may be available to some of you. Eligibility depends on the department you work in and on your individual circumstances, so please don't assume the arrangement will be approved automatically.

[04:14] AUDIO: I also want the holiday policy to be absolutely clear. Apart from official public holidays, apprentices must not arrange annual leave during the six-month program. You should take time away from work only if you're ill. If that condition is likely to cause a serious difficulty, speak to your supervisor.

[04:38] AUDIO: Your normal working week is 40 hours, though extra hours may be offered when the company is especially busy. Overtime isn't compulsory, but it gives you useful experience, so we recommend accepting it when you can. Of course, we realize that you may sometimes have commitments outside work, and it's fine to say you're unavailable on those occasions. As you know, there's no formal dress code.

[05:07] AUDIO: Casual clothes are acceptable, provided they're practical. For safety, the only footwear we don't permit is high heels, and we would actually prefer you to wear something comfortable, such as trainers. Finally, the canteen on-site is heavily subsidized, so hot meals and salads are inexpensive. We also provide drinks and snacks.

[05:32] AUDIO: Because of this, we've introduced a rule against bringing packed lunches into work. It encourages healthier eating and also prevents food being eaten at workstations, which isn't hygienic. Right, the next point is...

content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Cities Built By The Sea"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part 3. You will hear a tutor speaking to two students about their presentation on coastal cities. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

[00:53] TUTOR: I'd now like you to discuss your urban planning presentations with your partner. You should have completed most of the reading, so compare what you found decide how to organize a presentation and identify anything still to be done.
[01:10] CARLA: All right, Rob. I'm pleased we narrowed the topic to cities built beside the sea. That made it much easier to locate material that was directly relevant.
[01:21] ROB: Yes, urban populations are increasing very rapidly. In fact, more than half of the people in the world now live in cities.
[01:31] CARLA: True, but that figure covers every city, not only coastal ones. What surprised me was that most of the world's largest urban centers are on the coast.
[01:44] ROB: That was new to me too. A great many of them also stand where a river reaches the sea, and apparently that can cause difficulties.
[01:54] CARLA: In what way?

[01:56] ROB: As a city grows, farming and industrial development extend inland beside the river, pushing agriculture progressively farther upstream. That movement itself isn't necessarily harmful, but it results in increasing amounts of pollution entering the river.
[02:15] CARLA: And the current then carries those pollutants down towards the city?
[02:20] ROB: Exactly. Did you see the article about Miami on the eastern coast of the United States?
[02:27] CARLA: No, I didn't.
[02:28] ROB: It said that in the 1950s, channels were constructed to remove excess water whenever there was a risk of flooding.
[02:37] CARLA: That sounds like a reasonable solution.

[02:40] ROB: It did, and a considerable sum was spent on the project. The problem was that the designers didn't anticipate global warming. Because the channels were placed too near sea level, rising seas have made them almost ineffective. During heavy rain, the water has no route out, so the original design no longer works.
[03:04] CARLA: What are the authorities doing about the situation now?
[03:08] ROB: I'm not sure. I read that they intend to end the release of wastewater into the sea within the next decade.
[03:16] CARLA: But that doesn't solve the immediate flooding problem.
[03:20] ROB: No. For the short term, they need funding for a replacement drainage system to protect the city. Over a longer period, though, they have to consider the ecosystem as a whole.
[03:33] CARLA: Coastal cities can't resolve issues like these independently, can they? They need to coordinate what they do internationally, rather than each city acting in isolation.

[03:45] ROB: I agree. The problems are already well understood, and environmental specialists largely know which measures are needed, so lack of information isn't the main obstacle. The difficult part will be getting different countries to agree on the principles they will follow.
[04:05] CARLA: Yes. Assuming they ever reach that agreement.
[04:11] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
[04:57] CARLA: I think we now have enough material for the presentation. We only have 15 minutes after all.

[05:04] ROB: Then perhaps we should open with some historical context about why coastal cities developed. We shouldn't devote much time to it, because the other students will already know something about trade, transport links, and communication.
[05:20] CARLA: Agreed. We should also cover geographical features, such as wetlands, river estuaries, and coastal erosion. We could show maps of several cities with those features indicated.
[05:34] ROB: Were you thinking of putting the maps in a handout?
[05:38] CARLA: No. Slides that everyone can see would work better.
[05:43] ROB: We could examine past errors in more depth. Did you read the case study about the serious flooding in New Orleans some years ago?
[05:51] CARLA: Yes. Let's make that one case the basis of that part of the presentation. The others may not have read the study, but they'll remember the news reports about the flood.
[06:04] ROB: Fine. That should be enough background material.
[06:09] CARLA: After that, we can explain the steps currently being taken to address the difficulties facing coastal cities.
[06:16] ROB: What else should we include? Perhaps we need a section on future risks. Looking further ahead if city populations continue to increase.
[06:27] CARLA: Yes, but we'll have to investigate that. I don't have much information on it yet. Do you?
[06:35] ROB: No. We'll need to search online, though that shouldn't take very long.
[06:40] CARLA: Finally, we should discuss the international consequences. We might invite comments from the audience, since the class includes students from quite a range of places.
[06:52] ROB: That could be interesting, if time allows. Shall we move on to…
[07:01] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer discussing ways of producing renewable energy from the oceans. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Providing sufficient energy for our needs has become a major challenge.

[00:57] AUDIO: Demand is climbing quickly because the world's population is increasing and industry is expanding. At the same time, burning fossil fuels such as gas, coal and oil causes severe environmental damage and those resources will eventually be exhausted. Scientists have therefore spent years exploring ways to obtain power from renewable sources, including sunlight and wind, without producing pollution. In this talk, I'll introduce marine renewable energy, also known as ocean energy, which uses movement within the oceans.

[01:38] AUDIO: There are three broad forms of marine renewable energy. Wave energy, tidal energy and ocean thermal energy conversion. I'll briefly consider each of them, starting with wave energy. Many machines have been designed to capture power from waves, with names such as Wave Dragon, Penguin and Mighty Whale, and researchers are still looking for a truly efficient system.

[02:07] AUDIO: Wave power has considerable promise because the source is constant, the waves are never going to stop altogether. Electricity can be produced by offshore installations or by systems on land that use a reservoir. The difficulty is that ocean waves behave irregularly, wind can send them in any direction, which makes efficient equipment much harder to design. Ideally, the waves would move steadily along the same straight path.

[02:41] AUDIO: There is also an environmental concern. Devices may prevent sand and other sediment on the ocean floor from moving in its usual way. The next type is tidal energy. Compared with waves, tides have one important advantage.

[03:00] AUDIO: They are predictable, since the times of high and low tide can be calculated many years ahead. For tidal power to work well, there normally needs to be a difference of at least 5 meters between high and low tide, and only around 40 locations worldwide have that naturally. However, suitable conditions can be engineered by building a tidal lagoon, which is a body of seawater separated from the open sea. A proposed scheme in Wales would place such a lagoon in a bay at Swansea.

[03:36] AUDIO: A U-shaped breakwater, or dam, would extend from the coast around the water. 16 hydro turbines would be installed in it. As the tide comes in, water would pass rapidly through the breakwater and turn the turbines, which would drive a generator. When the tide begins to fall, water would be retained behind the breakwater for 3 hours.

[04:02] AUDIO: This would increase the difference in level until the lagoon stood several meters above the sea outside. The gates in the breakwater would then be opened, allowing the stored water to surge out. Its force would drive the turbines in the reverse direction and generate thousands of megawatts of electricity again. With two high tides each day, the lagoon could produce power four times daily, for roughly 14 hours out of every 24, supplying more than 150,000 homes.

[04:39] AUDIO: The design offers several benefits. Unlike wind and solar systems, it is not controlled by the weather. The turbines require no fuel, so they release no greenhouse gases, and they need very little maintenance. Forecasts suggest that power produced in this way would be fairly inexpensive.

[05:02] AUDIO: In addition, manufacturing the necessary parts could create more than 2,000 jobs and provide a substantial benefit to the local economy. There are concerns, however, that lagoons could damage fish and bird populations by disrupting migration patterns and allowing silt to accumulate, with consequences for nearby ecosystems. Other tidal technologies exist, but I'll now turn to the third category, ocean thermal energy conversion. This method requires a large temperature difference between surface water and water about two kilometers below it, a condition found in tropical coastal regions.
[05:47] AUDIO: Cold water is carried up through a submerged pipe. The principle was first proposed in 1881 when...

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a patient speaking to a doctor during her first appointment at a health clinic. First, you have some time to look at questions one to four. Now, listen carefully and answer questions one to four.
[00:50] CARL: Hello, come in and have a seat.
[00:52] JULIE: Thanks.
[00:53] CARL: I'm Carl Rogers, one of the doctors here at the Total Health Clinic. I understand this is your first appointment with us?
[01:01] JULIE: Yes, it is.
[01:04] CARL: Alright, I hope you'll be pleased with the care you receive here. If you don't mind, I'll take down a few details so that we can give you the most suitable service.
[01:13] JULIE: Of course.
[01:15] CARL: Let me begin by checking that your personal information is correct. We have your full name as Julianne Garcia.
[01:22] JULIE: Yes, that's right.
[01:23] CARL: Good. What's the best telephone number to reach you on?
[01:32] CARL: Thank you. And could I confirm your date of birth?
[01:36] JULIE: The 10th of October, 1992.
[01:39] CARL: Ah, our record says 1991. I'll change that now. Fine, I just need a little more personal information. Are you working at the moment, either full-time or part-time?
[01:51] JULIE: Yes, full-time. I work for Esterhazy's, the restaurant group. I joined them as a waitress a few years back, but I'm a manager now.
[02:03] CARL: I know the place. That's the branch on 114th Street, isn't it?
[02:08] JULIE: Yes, that's the one.
[02:10] CARL: I've eaten there several times. The salads are excellent.
[02:14] JULIE: I'm glad you like them.
[02:16] CARL: Before we discuss the reason for your visit, there's one final detail I need. The name of the company that provides your insurance.
[02:26] JULIE: It's Cawley Life Insurance, C-A-W-L-E-Y.
[02:32] CARL: Great, thank you.
[02:35] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 5 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 5 to 10.
[03:19] CARL: Now, Julie, let's talk about what we can do for you. What problem has brought you in today?
[03:27] JULIE: I've had some pain in my left knee. It wasn't too bad to begin with, but it's been getting worse, so I decided I should have it checked.
[03:36] CARL: That was sensible. When did you first become aware of it? Has it only been there for a few days, or longer?
[03:44] JULIE: Longer than that. It's become more painful over the past couple of days, but I first noticed it three weeks ago. It developed gradually, so I didn't pay much attention at first.
[03:59] CARL: Have you taken anything for it yourself, or tried any treatment?
[04:03] JULIE: I've used Tylenol for the pain. It helps for a few hours, but I don't want to rely on it too much.
[04:11] CARL: Have you tried treating it with heat?
[04:13] JULIE: No, though I've put ice on it for the last few days.
[04:17] CARL: Has that reduced the pain?
[04:19] JULIE: A little, yes.
[04:21] CARL: Good. You appear to be fairly fit in general.
[04:25] JULIE: Yes, I am.
[04:26] CARL: Do you take part in any sport regularly?
[04:29] JULIE: I play quite a lot of tennis. I'm a member of a club and go there often. I enjoy competing as much as the exercise, but I haven't played since the knee problem began.
[04:41] CARL: Do you do any other exercise?
[04:44] JULIE: I swim occasionally, mostly when I'm away on holiday. Normally, though, I go running three or four times a week.
[04:53] CARL: That puts a fair amount of strain on your legs. You've never had trouble with them before?
[04:59] JULIE: No, my legs have always been fine. I did slip in an accident last year and injure my shoulder, but that's fully recovered.
[05:09] CARL: Good. Are you allergic to anything?
[05:13] JULIE: No, not as far as I know.
[05:15] CARL: And do you take any medicine regularly?
[05:18] JULIE: Only vitamins. Apart from those, I don't take anything. I'm usually very healthy.
[05:24] CARL: Alright, let's examine the knee and see what may be causing the problem. Could you stand up for me?

passages.title: Visit To Branley Castle
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Visit To Branley Castle"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a guide giving visitors information about Branley Castle before they arrive. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15. We'll reach Branley Castle in about five minutes.

[00:52] AUDIO: Before we arrive, I'd like to tell you a little about its history and explain what you'll be able to see during the visit. There has been a castle on the site for more than 11 centuries. The earliest structure was a defensive fort built in 914 AD to protect the area from Danish raiders. It was commissioned by King Alfred the Great's daughter, who governed England at that time.

[01:15] AUDIO: In the next century, after the Norman Conquest, the estate was granted to a nobleman named Richard de Wehr. He put up a castle which remained in his family's hands for more than 400 years. By the time Queen Elizabeth I planned to stay there in 1576, the place was becoming rather neglected. Instead of refurbishing the existing guest chambers, the owners decided to build a separate timber residence for her beside the Great Hall.

[01:47] AUDIO: She spent four nights there in considerable comfort, although the building was lost in a fire only a few years later. During the 17th century, the wealthy Venice family owned the castle. They expanded it and introduced a number of improvements. By 1982, however, even with financial assistance from the state, the family could no longer meet the cost of looking after it, so they offered it for sale.

[02:18] AUDIO: The buyer was a business that already operated several amusement parks. Even so, when you enter the castle, I think you'll find that its historic character has been carefully preserved. In the state apartments, you'll see remarkably realistic wax figures wearing clothes from different periods. They don't simply stand still.

[02:42] AUDIO: The figures move and appear to talk to one another. Each room also contains a booklet explaining its former purpose and describing the furniture and objects on display. The grounds cover a large area. Sheep once grazed there, and during the 19th century the owners kept a small zoo, with creatures ranging from rabbits to a young elephant.

[03:09] AUDIO: Those former animal buildings now house exhibitions of paintings and sculpture. The park still has many fine trees, though its oldest one, which had survived for 800 years, was brought down by a storm in 1987. You're welcome to explore independently until half past four. At that time, we'll gather at the foot of the Great Staircase.

[03:36] AUDIO: From there, we'll visit the Long Gallery, where photographs show the family who lived here a century ago enjoying tea and cakes in the Conservatory. We'll then go to that same Conservatory where refreshments will be served to our group. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Woolly Mammoths On St Paul’s Island"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students discussing a presentation about woolly mammoths with their tutor. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:51] TUTOR: Right, Rosie and Martin, let's see how far you've got with your presentation on woolly mammoths.
[00:58] ROSIE: Sure, we've brought along a brief plan.
[01:02] TUTOR: Thanks. Your main focus is a research study in North America, is that right?

[01:09] MARTIN: Yes, though, we thought the opening should give some background first. We'll explain that woolly mammoths were relatives of today's elephants, and lived during the last ice age, many thousands of years ago.

[01:24] ROSIE: We considered starting with a short extract from a cartoon about mammoths, but it might seem rather childish. A diagram could work better. Perhaps a timeline with pictures to show the period when they lived.
[01:39] MARTIN: What about a sketch of a herd crossing the ice? Actually, no. Your timeline idea would introduce the topic more effectively.
[01:49] TUTOR: Good. After that, you cover the mammoth tooth discovered on St. Paul's Island in Alaska, and explain why the find mattered.

[02:00] ROSIE: That's right. Russell Graham found the tooth beneath a rock in a cave. It was exceptionally well preserved. It looked almost as though it had only recently been taken from the animal's jaw.
[02:16] ROSIE: Tests showed that it was about 6,500 years old.
[02:21] TUTOR: And why was that result important?
[02:23] ROSIE: Because mammoth remains previously discovered on the North American mainland dated from much earlier. Finding such a comparatively recent tooth was extraordinary.

[02:36] MARTIN: Then we'll use an animated graphic to reconstruct the region in prehistoric times. At first, St. Paul's was joined to the mainland, so mammoths, bears, and other animals could move freely across the whole area.
[02:51] ROSIE: As the climate became warmer, sea levels rose and the land connection disappeared. The mammoths were left cut off on the new island, with no route back to the mainland.
[03:04] MARTIN: They actually continued living there for several thousand years after mammoths had vanished from the mainland.
[03:12] TUTOR: Do researchers know what caused the mainland population to disappear?
[03:17] ROSIE: No. There isn't a definite explanation.

[03:21] MARTIN: Next we'll describe how Graham's team worked out when the island mammoths became extinct. They placed it at 5,600 years ago, which is unusually precise for an event in prehistory. Their evidence came from material collected in the mud at the bottom of an island lake. By examining the layers, they could identify plant fragments, volcanic ash, and even mammoth DNA deposited over time.
[03:52] MARTIN: The method itself is routine, although analyzing the samples took almost two years.
[04:01] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
[04:48] TUTOR: Why don't you now review the main sections of the presentation and decide what still has to be done for each one?
[04:56] MARTIN: All right. For the introduction, we're planning to use that visual. So once we've made it, I suppose the section is finished.

[05:06] ROSIE: I'm not convinced. We should prepare detailed notes covering every point we want to mention rather than trusting ourselves to remember it all. The opening matters too much to improvise.
[05:19] MARTIN: Yes, I agree.

[05:20] ROSIE: The discovery of the tooth is probably the most striking part, but our only source so far is that article we found online, and it doesn't give us much detail. Perhaps we could contact the scientist who directed the research and ask for some additional information.
[05:39] MARTIN: That sounds useful. What should we do with the section about the researcher's original questions? We've gathered plenty of material, but we need a lively way to present it.
[05:50] ROSIE: We could invite the audience to propose questions of their own. Then check how many our presentation can answer. It shouldn't take very long.
[06:00] TUTOR: Yes, that would make the session more varied.
[06:05] MARTIN: Then there's the later work on the island, particularly the analysis of the lake mud. We may have included too much. Do you think some of it should be removed?
[06:17] ROSIE: I'd keep the information, but the way it's arranged is confusing at the moment.
[06:22] MARTIN: In that case, we could put the research stages into chronological order.
[06:27] ROSIE: Agreed. The section on the results and possible interpretations is nearly complete, although we ought to rehearse it and check that it stays within the allotted time.
[06:39] MARTIN: It will probably fit, but we should confirm that.
[06:42] TUTOR: For the final section on its significance today, you've collected some strong ideas. What's missing is your own interpretation, rather than another summary of other people's views.
[06:59] MARTIN: Understood. We'll work on that. Shall we now?
[07:04] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer discussing the early development of weather forecasting. You will hear a lecturer discussing the early development of weather forecasting. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

[00:58] AUDIO: In this lecture series on the history of weather prediction, today's talk will concentrate on the earliest stages. So, let's begin several thousand years ago. Most ancient societies had gods associated with the weather and disasters such as floods often appeared in stories about the creation of the world. In general, people explained weather as the result of divine moods.

[01:27] AUDIO: The variety of weather deities reflects this idea. The Egyptians, for example, worshipped the sun god Ra, while in Norse tradition Thor controlled thunder and lightning. Many early civilizations performed rituals, including dances, in the hope that the weather gods would treat them favourably. Yet weather also affected everyday life.

[01:54] AUDIO: People had to watch the sky and interpret what they saw correctly. Their survival could depend on it. We don't know when systematic observation began, but by about 650 BC the Babylonians were producing short-term forecasts from changes in clouds and other natural signs. The Chinese also identified recurring patterns.

[02:20] AUDIO: By 300 BC their astronomers had created a calendar dividing the year into 24 festivals, each linked with a particular weather event. The Greeks, however, were the first to seek a more scientific explanation. A particularly important figure was the philosopher and scientist Aristotle, whose thinking remained influential for almost two millennia. In 340 BC he wrote a work that tried to explain the development of rain, clouds, winds and storms.

[03:00] AUDIO: He also discussed phenomena in the heavens, including halos, bright rings around the sun, moon or luminous stars, as well as comets. A surprising number of his observations were correct. For instance, he understood that heat could turn water into vapour. On the other hand, Aristotle also reached several false conclusions, among them the claim that the Earth breathed out the winds.

[03:33] AUDIO: Mistakes of this kind began to be corrected during and after the Renaissance. Even so, his writings were treated as the main authority on weather for nearly 2,000 years. During the Middle Ages, observations were also preserved in sayings. One familiar example is the proverb about a red sky bringing fine weather at night, but warning of poor weather in the morning.

[04:04] AUDIO: Modern meteorologists have found that many such sayings grew from careful observation and can be reliable. For centuries, forecasts depended entirely on what individuals could observe for themselves. In the 15th century though, scientists began to recognise the need for instruments. Before that, they had little beyond wind vanes used to establish wind direction and simple rain gauges.

[04:37] AUDIO: An early addition was the hygrometer invented in the 15th century to measure moisture in the air. It was one of a series of devices that advanced weather forecasting. Then, in 1592, the Italian scientist and inventor Galileo produced the first thermometer. Galileo's pupil Torricelli later devised the barometer, making it possible to measure air pressure.

[05:09] AUDIO: In 1648, the French philosopher Pascal demonstrated that pressure falls as altitude rises. The English astronomer Halley confirmed this finding in 1686, and he was also the first to chart the trade winds. As scientists became better able to measure weather-related factors, their understanding of the atmosphere and its processes improved, and observations began to be recorded systematically. In the 18th century, the scientist and politician Benjamin Franklin investigated electricity, particularly lightning, but weather remained an interest throughout most of his life.

[05:59] AUDIO: Franklin established that storms generally move from west to east. Progress in understanding the atmosphere also depended on developments beyond new measuring devices. Observers in separate places started keeping records, and in the middle of the 19th century, the telegraph allowed their information to be brought together. By the end of that century, this had led to the first organised weather services.
[06:31] AUDIO: Mathematics and physics did not become established parts of meteorology until the early 20th century, and that is where we will continue next week. That is the end of part four.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a man asking the customer services manager of a hotel about facilities for a conference. You will hear a man asking the customer services manager of a hotel about facilities for a conference. First, you have some time to look at questions one to five. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to five.
[00:57] ANGELA: Good morning, Flanders Conference Hotel.
[01:00] MAN: Hello. I'm calling to inquire about the hotel's conference facilities. Are you the right person to speak to?
[01:10] ANGELA: Yes, I'm the customer services manager. My name's Angela. How can I help?
[01:17] MAN: I'm with Barrett and Stansons. We're a medical firm based in Melbourne.
[01:22] ANGELA: Right, yes.
[01:23] MAN: We're arranging a two-day conference in Sydney for some of our clients and we expect roughly 50 to 60 delegates.
[01:32] ANGELA: Do you have any dates in mind?
[01:34] MAN: We were thinking of early next year, perhaps the final weekend in January. It does need to be held at a weekend.
[01:43] ANGELA: Let me check. The conference area is taken for the weekend starting on January the 28th. The first weekend in February is still free though.
[01:54] MAN: Would January the 21st work?
[01:57] ANGELA: Sorry, that weekend has already been reserved as well.
[02:01] MAN: All right, then we'll choose the February weekend.
[02:04] ANGELA: That will be the weekend beginning February the 4th.
[02:08] MAN: Fine. Could you describe the conference facilities you offer?
[02:14] ANGELA: Certainly. Talks and presentations can be held in the Tesla room.
[02:18] MAN: Could you repeat the name?
[02:21] ANGELA: Tesla. T-E-S-L-A. The room can seat as many as a hundred people and has a projector and the usual presentation equipment.
[02:32] MAN: Is there a microphone?
[02:34] ANGELA: Yes. One will be prepared for the speaker and there's another available for audience questions if you need it.
[02:42] MAN: Good. We'll also want a fairly large open space where people can sit with coffee. We're planning an exhibition of our products and services in the same area.
[02:54] ANGELA: That won't be a problem. The central atrium can accommodate both and you may come in before the conference to set up the displays.
[03:03] MAN: Excellent. I assume there's Wi-Fi as well.
[03:08] ANGELA: Yes, it's free and can be used everywhere in the hotel.
[03:13] MAN: Great.
[03:14] ANGELA: Would you like the hotel to arrange a buffet lunch too? We offer a two-course meal with several choices.
[03:22] MAN: How much would that cost?
[03:24] ANGELA: I can email our standard menu which is priced at $45 a person. There's also a special menu that costs $25 more.
[03:34] MAN: The standard one should be sufficient but please send me a copy of the menu.
[03:41] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
[04:26] MAN: We'll also require rooms on the Saturday night for some delegates. I can't confirm the number yet but it will probably be around 25. What is the room rate?
[04:37] ANGELA: Conference guests receive a 25% discount so their rooms will be $135. The usual price for a standard room is $180.
[04:50] MAN: Does the reduced rate include breakfast?
[04:53] ANGELA: Yes, it does. Guests may also use the rest of the hotel's facilities. There's a spa offering treatments such as massages and facials and a pool on the roof for hotel residents.
[05:07] MAN: That sounds good. How easy is it to reach the hotel? You're in the city center, aren't you?
[05:15] ANGELA: Yes. The airport is about 12 kilometers away and hotel guests can take our complimentary shuttle. The central railway station is also only a 10-minute walk.
[05:27] MAN: Fine. I'm not very familiar with Sydney, so could you explain exactly where the hotel is?

[05:36] ANGELA: It's in the city center on Wilby Street, which is a small road quite close to the sea. If delegates want to go out on Saturday evening, there are plenty of restaurants nearby. They can continue to one of the many clubs in the district afterwards if they want a late night.
[05:54] MAN: Alright. If we decide to book, could you tell me how much that is?

passages.title: What volunteers have helped people to do
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "What volunteers have helped people to do"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear the director of a local volunteering organization explaining what volunteers do and how people benefit. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Good morning, I'm Lucy Crittenden, the director of operations for an organization that coordinates voluntary work in this region.

[01:08] AUDIO: I'm hoping that by the end of this talk, I may have encouraged one or two of you to volunteer as well. I'll begin with a quick explanation of what volunteering involves. Volunteers are young people or adults who freely give some of their time without being paid to support others. Most people who volunteer spend two or three hours a week on it, although some contribute considerably more.

[01:38] AUDIO: Those receiving help may, for instance, have physical conditions or difficulties with their behavior. The work volunteers do varies widely and depends on what they're good at and what interests them. Suppose a family is having a hard time. A volunteer might offer advice about preparing food, organizing household spending, or making sensible choices when buying groceries.

[02:06] AUDIO: They could also help to paint or put up wallpaper, perhaps working alongside family members who are able to join in. Another possibility is looking after the children for a while, which gives the parents an opportunity to go out. And the advantages don't all go to the people receiving support. Volunteers benefit, too.

[02:30] AUDIO: They put their abilities to use while helping someone manage mental or physical ill health. Volunteering can also strengthen a CV when they apply for work, since employers generally respond positively to applicants who have chosen to give their time to others. Perhaps most importantly, the majority of volunteers say the work provides a real sense of direction in their lives. I think they're fortunate to have that, because plenty of people never find it.

[03:06] AUDIO: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. I'd now like to share what several of our volunteers have said about their roles so you can see the different ways they support people. Habib works with an older woman who is starting to experience dementia.

[04:05] AUDIO: Once a week, the two of them join other elderly people at the community center, where visitors lead a singing session. The familiar songs bring back memories of when the listeners were younger, and for a short time, their present-day problems fade into the background. Consuela is a remarkable woman. Walking is difficult for her, but she refuses to be limited by it.

[04:32] AUDIO: She supports two people who had similar trouble getting around and had almost given up walking. Because they can see what she manages herself, she inspires them to walk a little farther and more often. Minh visits a young man who lives by himself and cannot go out alone, so he used to have very little contact with anyone. Now they go to films together, or call on friends whom the young man had been unable to see for a long time.

[05:05] AUDIO: Tanya calls on an elderly woman every week. When the woman learned that Tanya worked professionally as a dressmaker, she became curious. Tanya showed her a few soft toys she had made, and the woman decided to have a go herself. She now spends hours making them, and gets enormous enjoyment from this new activity, even if her work has not quite reached Tanya's standard yet.

[05:33] AUDIO: Alexei volunteers with a family dealing with several problems. He discusses possible ways forward with them in a calm manner, helping them understand that they can take action themselves rather than remain powerless. That change has made a major difference to their confidence. Finally, although there are many others I could mention, there's Juba.

[05:59] AUDIO: She supports a teenage girl with learning difficulties, who used to find conversation very hard. Juba has worked patiently with her, and the girl can now explain herself much more clearly and understand what other people are saying. I hope those examples have shown you what volunteering can involve. Now I'd like...
[06:25] AUDIO: That is the end of part two.

passages.title: Background on school marching band
content: 📌 Background on school marching band

The band contains approximately [ _____ ] pupils.
It will compete in a [ _____ ] band contest.
The band has been asked to perform at the town's [ _____ ].
The pupils have heard a recorded speech given by a [ _____ ].
Joe intends to discuss a [ _____ ] with the band.
Joe would like some members to attend a [ _____ ] next month.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two trainee, you will hear two trainee teachers discussing Joe's work with a school marching band. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
[00:53] LIZZIE: How are things going with your teaching placement at the high school Joe?
[00:57] JOE: Well, I've been asked to run the school marching band and it is a considerable responsibility. I'd like to talk it through with you.
[01:06] LIZZIE: Of course, perhaps you should begin by giving me some background.

[01:11] JOE: Right. The band includes pupils from every year group so their ages range from 11 to 18 and there are roughly 50 members altogether. It is a popular school activity. The largest band I've worked with before had only 20 players so this feels very different.
[01:33] LIZZIE: That must be quite a change.

[01:35] JOE: They are not yet at the standard needed for national band competitions but they have entered a regional competition later this term. I'm not expecting them to win, but I hope taking part will encourage them to raise their level.
[01:51] LIZZIE: Yes, it should give them something to aim for.

[01:54] JOE: The town council is also arranging a carnival this summer and the band has been invited to perform there. At the moment I don't think they are ready so I need to get them playing more effectively as one group and I haven't got much time.
[02:11] LIZZIE: Have you tried anything apart from rehearsing the pieces?

[02:15] JOE: I found a recording of a drummer describing how joining a band had transformed his life. I think it came from an after dinner speech. I found it inspiring because music had kept him away from crime and the pupils appeared interested as well.
[02:34] LIZZIE: That sounds encouraging.
[02:37] JOE: Next I'm planning to show them the old 1940s film Strike Up the Band and then discuss it with them. Does that seem worthwhile?
[02:48] LIZZIE: Definitely. Because it centers on a school band it may help them see what they could accomplish by cooperating.

[02:55] JOE: Exactly. I'd also like to take some of the band to a parade next month. Two marching bands are due to perform so the atmosphere should be lively. It will depend on whether I can convince the school to pay for one or two coaches.
[03:10] LIZZIE: Those all sound like useful ideas.
[03:14] JOE: Thanks.
[03:18] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
[04:02] JOE: Could I tell you about a few band members I'm finding difficult to manage? I'm sure you can suggest what I might do.
[04:10] LIZZIE: Go ahead.

[04:10] JOE: One of the flautists insists that she loves being in the band. We rehearse after school twice a week but she is almost never present. She finds me the following day and offers a convincing explanation. Such as needing to help her mother or being unwell but honestly I don't believe her.
[04:33] LIZZIE: Oh dear. Are there any other troublesome students?

[04:36] JOE: Quite a few. There is a trumpeter who considers herself the strongest musician in the band although she certainly isn't. She is constantly telling the other players what they ought to do which makes leading the group very difficult.
[04:54] LIZZIE: She sounds hard to deal with.

[04:56] JOE: She is. Then there is a trombonist with an excellent sense of rhythm who could become a very good musician. The problem is that he has a breathing condition and cannot produce enough air for the trombone. Percussion would suit him much better but he refuses to change so he manages only some of the notes.
[05:19] LIZZIE: I suppose his determination is admirable.

[05:23] JOE: Perhaps. One of the percussionists plays reasonably well but he keeps apart from everyone else and leaves immediately when each rehearsal finishes. There may be difficulties at home. I really don't know.
[05:39] JOE: Still it is a concern in a band where everyone needs to feel part of the group.
[05:44] LIZZIE: I see.
[05:45] JOE: There are a few more but that gives you a sense of the situation. What would you advise me to do Lizzie?
[05:56] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers.
