passages.title: Concerts in university arts festival
content: 📌 Concerts in university arts festival

Concert 1
Australian composer: Liza Lim

before she began composing, she learnt both piano and [ _____ ]orchestras, performers and festivals worldwide have commissioned many of her worksher compositions convey considerable [ _____ ] and draw on several cultural traditionsher music is very expressive although it is also [ _____ ]the festival will present her seven-part [ _____ ], The OresteiaLim described the sounds used in The Oresteia as [ _____ ]
British composers: Ralph Vaughan Williams, Frederick Delius

Concert 2
British composers: Benjamin Britten, Judith Weir
Australian composer: Ross Edwards

the festival includes The Tower of Remoteness, which was inspired by natureThe Tower of Remoteness was composed for piano and [ _____ ]his output includes pieces for childrenhis music celebrates the cultural [ _____ ] of Australia

Concert 3
Australian composer: Carl Vine

played the cornet before changing to the pianofirst studied [ _____ ] at university, then moved to musicworked independently in Sydney as a pianist and composergained recognition for creating music for [ _____ ]the festival programme contains his music for the 1996 [ _____ ]
British composers: Edward Elgar, Thomas Adès
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer describing, you will hear a lecturer describing three concerts arranged for a University Arts Festival. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. You already know that the University is organizing an Arts Festival later this year.

[00:59] AUDIO: Here in the Music Department, we have now finalized the program for three public concerts. The festival explores connections between Britain and Australia, so every concert combines music by composers from both countries. Since the Australian works may be less familiar to you, I will give you a brief introduction to them. Concert 1 includes music by Liza Lim, who was born in Perth in Western Australia in 1966.

[01:37] AUDIO: When Lim was young, she learnt the piano and the violin, as many children do. At 11, however, her teachers persuaded her to try writing music, and she soon realized that composition was where her real ability lay. She went on to study the subject and later taught it in Australia and overseas. Orchestras, individual performers and festivals in a number of countries have commissioned her work.

[02:13] AUDIO: Her compositions are full of energy, and she frequently draws on Asian traditions and Aboriginal Australian culture. One example is the compass, which features the didgeridoo. Her music is highly expressive, and even though it is complex, it communicates strongly with performers and audiences. For the festival, we will present a semi-staged version of the Oresteia.

[02:45] AUDIO: The Oresteia is an opera in seven sections, derived from Aeschylus's trilogy of ancient Greek tragedies. Lim composed it while she was still in her mid-twenties, and shared responsibility for the text with Barikoski. Six vocalists and a dancer perform with an orchestra whose instruments include an electric guitar and a traditional Turkish stringed instrument, as well as the usual orchestral forces. Lim explained that the stories themselves are difficult to relate, so the sounds she created are disturbing too.

[03:28] AUDIO: They incorporate breathing, crying, laughter, and whistling. The piece runs for about 75 minutes. The rest of Concert 1 consists of orchestral music by the British composers Ralph Vaughan Williams and Frederick Delius. Concert 2 opens with instrumental works by the British composers Benjamin Britten and Judith Weir.

[04:01] AUDIO: Following the interval, the focus shifts to Australia, with Ross Edwards's The Tower of Remoteness. Edwards said that nature inspired the piece. He had been sitting by himself in a dry creek bed, beneath palm leaves, listening to insects and birds. The music is written for piano and clarinet.

[04:31] AUDIO: Only years later did Edwards recognize that he had unconsciously based its opening phrase on the call of a bird. Edwards was born in Sydney in 1943. He studied at the Sydney Conservatorium of Music and at the Universities of Adelaide and Sydney. He is one of Australia's most frequently performed composers and has produced music in many forms, including symphonies, concertos, and works intended specifically for children.

[05:07] AUDIO: His music is often said to have a profound connection with Australia, and it celebrates the diversity of the country's cultures. The third Australian composer in our festival is Carl Vine. Like Lisa Lim, Vine comes from Perth in Western Australia. He was born in 1954 and started playing the cornet when he was five, moving to the piano at ten.

[05:39] AUDIO: At university, though, he initially studied physics before transferring to composition. After completing his degree, he settled in Sydney and worked independently as both a pianist and a composer. He soon established a reputation in Australia for composing music for dance and has written 25 scores in that field. In concert three, we will perform Vine's music for the flag handover ceremony at the 1996 Olympics.

[06:17] AUDIO: This orchestral work lasts seven minutes and was heard by millions of people around the world. It will appear in the programme with music by the British composers Edward Elgar and, from a later generation, Thomas Ades. That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part 1 You will hear a woman speaking to a hotel events manager about arranging an anniversary celebration. First, you have some time to look at questions one to seven. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to seven.
[00:55] ANDREW: Good morning, Clare House Hotel. Andrew speaking. I'm the events manager.

[01:01] SAM: Good morning, Andrew. I'm Samantha. I'm organising a celebration for my parents' 50th wedding anniversary and I'm calling to ask about booking a function room for some time next September. My parents and a number of the guests will also need somewhere to stay.
[01:21] ANDREW: Of course. We should be able to arrange that. Are you thinking of a seated meal or something less formal?
[01:29] SAM: Most likely a sit-down meal.
[01:31] ANDREW: Have you got an idea of the number attending?
[01:34] SAM: I'd say roughly 80.
[01:36] ANDREW: In that case, there are two rooms large enough. The Adelphi room accommodates 85 people for a seated meal and more than 100 if it's a standing reception.
[01:48] SAM: That sounds fine.

[01:50] ANDREW: If you decide on live music, there's a gallery overlooking the room with enough space for four or five musicians. People like it because the music carries well enough for dancing without making conversation impossible.
[02:06] SAM: Good. I hate having to shout just to speak to someone.
[02:10] ANDREW: Quite. The Adelphi is at the rear of the hotel with French windows opening onto a terrace. In September, there are lots of pots there filled with roses.
[02:22] SAM: Which way does the terrace face?
[02:24] ANDREW: It faces southwest so it catches the sun through the afternoon and into the early evening.
[02:33] SAM: That would be lovely.
[02:35] ANDREW: The terrace looks across a cluster of trees in the hotel grounds. You can walk through them to the river, although the river itself is too far away to be seen from the hotel.
[02:47] SAM: I see.

[02:48] ANDREW: The other possibility is the Carlton room. It's slightly larger and can take up to 110 people. It also has a stage which is useful for entertainment and a small band can perform there as well.
[03:03] SAM: Does that room open onto an outdoor area?
[03:07] ANDREW: No. It's on the first floor, but the windows along one side look over the lake.
[03:13] SAM: Nice. Either room could work for us.
[03:16] ANDREW: Would you like me to explain some of the additional services we provide?
[03:21] SAM: Yes, please.
[03:23] ANDREW: Along with the meal, you can book a master of ceremonies or MC who remains with you throughout the event.
[03:31] SAM: What would the MC actually do? If we wanted someone to make a speech during the meal, would that be part of the role?

[03:40] ANDREW: Yes. Our MCs are trained public speakers so they have no trouble being heard over a busy room. There also there is your support. If any problem comes up, the MC handles it and you don't have to worry.
[03:56] SAM: That's useful. I'll ask about the menu in a moment, but accommodation matters too. I know the hotel has bedrooms, but is there anything else, perhaps cabins?
[04:09] ANDREW: There are five cabins in the grounds. Each one is self-contained, sleeps between two and four people, and includes a living area, bathroom and small kitchen.
[04:21] SAM: That would suit us very well.
[04:26] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions eight to ten. Now listen and answer questions eight to ten.
[05:12] SAM: You have several leisure facilities, don't you? Are they all covered by the room hire charge? I was wondering about the outdoor pool, for example.

[05:21] ANDREW: Guests can normally use it, but unfortunately it will be closed for refurbishment for the whole of September. The gym will still be open though, and using it doesn't cost anything extra. It's available from six in the morning until midnight.
[05:39] SAM: Alright.

[05:40] ANDREW: The tennis courts will be open too, although there's a small additional charge for those. We have four courts, and it's sensible to reserve one early, because the waiting list can get quite long.
[05:56] SAM: Understood. Could we talk about the food now? We'd be planning dinner for about seven o'clock.
[06:05] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: Part 2. You will hear a hotel representative explaining the excursions and evening entertainment available to guests. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.
[00:58] AUDIO: Hello, everyone. I'm Jake Stevens, the hotel representative. I hope you're enjoying your stay. Let me start with the excursions available to guests this week.

[01:11] AUDIO: Dolphin watching is something you really shouldn't miss. The boat leaves every day and the trip costs 35 euros. We are so confident that dolphins will appear that anyone who does not see them may take the trip again without paying. Today's afternoon sailing has no places left, though, so speak to me about another day.

[01:34] AUDIO: For more active guests, there is also our forest walk. The guided forest route is about seven kilometers. We stop halfway and provide a drink and sandwiches. Some sections climb quite steeply, so participants should be reasonably fit, wear suitable shoes and carry a waterproof in case it rains.

[01:58] AUDIO: The Wednesday walk costs 25 euros with everything included. On Thursday, we run a cycling excursion that offers the pleasure of riding without a difficult climb. We transport both you and your bicycle to the top of Mount Larna, then you ride back down. The route drops 700 meters over only 20 kilometers, so it is not intended for inexperienced cyclists because speeds can be high.

[02:29] AUDIO: In clear weather, the views are excellent. Our local craft tour introduces traditional island industries. There is no charge for this excursion. It includes a jewelry workshop and a ceramic center, where you may buy products, if you wish, although purchases are entirely optional.

[02:51] AUDIO: It leaves after lunch on Thursday and returns by six in the evening. The island is also an outstanding place for looking at the night sky. On Friday, our 90 euro observatory excursion includes the large telescopes and an explanation by a specialist of how they operate. Afterwards, we go down to Sunset Beach, where anyone who wants to can swim in the sea before the return journey.

[03:22] AUDIO: Finally, horse riding is arranged through the equestrian center near Playa Cortino. It suits keen riders as well as people who have never ridden before. The route reaches the beach, allowing riders to canter across the sand and through the edge of the waves. It costs 35 euros and is offered every day.

[03:47] AUDIO: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. There is plenty to do during the day, but we also have evening entertainment. The most popular event is Musical Favorites.

[04:41] AUDIO: It includes a three-course dinner and as many drinks as you want, all in the ticket price. The show begins with songs from Paris-based musicals, moves to Las Vegas, and finishes at Copacabana. After the performance, the cast come down from the stage in costume so guests can talk to them. Demand is very high, so reserve a place in advance rather than waiting until the final moment.

[05:11] AUDIO: It takes place on Friday. Tickets cost 50 euros each and a table beside the stage costs another 10 euros. For a journey into the past, choose Saturday's Castle Feast. Dinner is served in the courtyard of a 12th-century castle by attendants wearing long gowns.

[05:33] AUDIO: Each visitor receives a whole chicken and eats it in the medieval manner with their hands rather than knives and forks. The entertainment includes mounted contests in which riders try to knock one another from their horses. Later, you can watch Dancing in the Ballroom and join the dancers yourself if you wish. Now, if anyone...

passages.title: Trevor and Stephanie
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Trevor and Stephanie"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear Trevor and Stephanie discussing a course on children's literature. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
[00:54] STEPHANIE: Hi, Trevor.
[00:56] TREVOR: Hi, Stephanie. You wanted to ask me about the children's literature course I'm doing, didn't you?
[01:01] STEPHANIE: Yes. I'm considering taking it next year, but I wanted to know a bit more about it first.
[01:09] TREVOR: Sure. As you probably know, it lasts for a year. There are six compulsory modules, and the one I found especially interesting looked at the purpose of literature written for children.
[01:22] STEPHANIE: So, whether stories are simply meant to entertain, or whether they should teach children as well?

[01:30] TREVOR: Exactly. And whether that teaching is factual, giving children knowledge about the world, or ethical, passing on values. What interested me was that authors themselves may not realize what values their stories communicate. A child in a story might get into trouble after ignoring an adult, for example, which suggests that children should always do as they're told.
[01:56] STEPHANIE: I see what you mean.

[01:59] TREVOR: That module showed me how strongly stories can influence children as they grow up. In fact, it encouraged me to try writing a children's story myself, just as a personal project. I know I couldn't match hugely popular books such as the Harry Potter series. They're excellent.
[02:20] TREVOR: And even younger readers like my seven-year-old niece enjoy them.
[02:24] STEPHANIE: I'm particularly interested in illustrations. Does the course cover those?
[02:30] TREVOR: Yes, there's a module on pictures, including the way they can sometimes be central to a story.

[02:37] STEPHANIE: That's good. I can still picture some frightening illustrations I saw when I was little, even after all these years. Images can be every bit as powerful as words. I've always loved drawing, and I'd like to work as an illustrator after the course, so that module should be very useful.

[02:59] TREVOR: I'm sure it will. We considered comics in that module, too, although I don't think they have the same value as books. With words, readers have to form the scenes in their own minds, whereas a comic provides the images for them.

[03:17] STEPHANIE: But children already receive so much visual information from television, games, and similar media. Some of them wouldn't attempt a conventional book at all, so comics can perform a genuinely useful role.
[03:33] TREVOR: You mean reading a comic is preferable to reading nothing? Yes, I suppose you're right. I still think it's unfortunate when children never read books.
[03:45] STEPHANIE: Does the course also discuss books written specifically for girls or for boys?

[03:51] TREVOR: Yes, that's another module. For a long time, many English-language stories showed boys having adventures while girls remained at home playing with dolls. I was astonished by how many books were directed at one sex only rather than at both. Naturally, that reflected the society in which those books were produced.
[04:15] STEPHANIE: True. It sounds as if you would recommend the course.
[04:24] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
[05:10] TREVOR: Have you been reading many children's stories to help you decide whether to enroll?
[05:16] STEPHANIE: Yes. I've gone back as far as the late 17th century, although I know children's stories existed before then.
[05:25] TREVOR: Does that include Perot's fairy tales such as Cinderella and The Sleeping Beauty?
[05:31] STEPHANIE: It does. They're significant because nothing quite like them had appeared before. They established a new kind of story. I also read The Swiss Family Robinson.
[05:43] TREVOR: I haven't read that one.

[05:46] STEPHANIE: The English title makes Robinson sound like the family's surname. A closer translation would be The Swiss Robinsons, because the story concerns a Swiss family shipwrecked in a situation resembling Robinson Crusoe, the title of a novel published a century earlier.
[06:05] TREVOR: I had no idea.
[06:08] STEPHANIE: Have you read Hoffman's The Nutcracker and the Mouse King?
[06:13] TREVOR: Isn't that the story that inspired Tchaikovsky's ballet The Nutcracker?
[06:17] STEPHANIE: Yes. That's the one. Some parts of it are rather strange.
[06:24] TREVOR: I hope you've read Oscar Wilde's The Happy Prince. It's probably my favorite children's story.

[06:30] STEPHANIE: Mine too. It's unexpected because Wilde is mainly known for his witty plays, while The Happy Prince is deeply moving. I had a much harder time with Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings. There are three long volumes, and I stopped after the first.
[06:49] TREVOR: Even so, it's enormously popular.
[06:53] STEPHANIE: Yes, but The Happy Prince drew me in immediately. Whereas The Lord of the Rings demanded more effort than I was willing to give it.
[07:02] TREVOR: That wasn't my experience. I love it.
[07:06] STEPHANIE: Another book I've read is War Horse.
[07:09] TREVOR: That's set during the First World War, isn't it? War seems an unlikely subject for a children's story.
[07:17] STEPHANIE: Exactly, but it has been very successful. Have you read any?
[07:26] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answer.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer discussing marine archaeology and the technology used to investigate submerged sites. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Today I want to introduce marine archaeology, the area of marine archaeology concerned with the ways people have interacted with oceans, lakes and rivers.

[01:04] AUDIO: It examines vessels, their cargoes, harbour structures and other material remains. I'll begin with one example, then explain how recent technology is changing this research. Atlet Yam was a community on the eastern Mediterranean coast which appears to have prospered until roughly 7000 BC. Its inhabitants raised cattle, fished and kept stores of grain.

[01:32] AUDIO: They drew fresh water from wells and many stone houses were arranged around courtyards. The village also had a remarkable monument, seven stones, each weighing about half a tonne set in a semicircle around a natural spring. It may have served a ceremonial purpose. Atlet Yam could have been overwhelmed suddenly by a tsunami or gradually flooded when a warmer climate melted glaciers and raised sea levels.

[02:03] AUDIO: Whatever happened, the site now rests ten metres beneath the Mediterranean, covered by sand. It has been called the largest and best preserved prehistoric settlement discovered on the seabed. For marine archaeologists, the site offers an extraordinary amount of evidence. By studying its buildings, tools and human remains, researchers have learned how this busy community operated and even identified illnesses suffered by some residents.

[02:36] AUDIO: Yet one village provides only a narrow view of a vanished world. A broader picture requires more submerged settlements and locating them is the real challenge. In the past, divers had to search for wrecks and artefacts themselves. During the second half of the 20th century, several kinds of underwater vehicle appeared.

[03:00] AUDIO: Some were directed from a surface ship, while autonomous models could operate without a human controller. Autonomous underwater vehicles, usually called AUVs, have long been used by the oil industry to produce maps of the seabed before rigs and pipelines are put in place. They navigate with instruments such as compasses and sonar. Until fairly recently, these machines cost a great deal and were so heavy that a winch on a large vessel was needed to lower them into the water.

[03:36] AUDIO: Newer AUVs are far easier to handle and can be launched from the shore or a small boat. Their lower price also puts them within reach of more research teams. They are highly advanced as well. Several vehicles can exchange information and decide, for example, how to divide a survey efficiently or locate particular objects.

[04:01] AUDIO: Trials have shown that this cooperative method works. In 2015, three AUVs searched for wrecks at Marsa Memi, near Sicily. An ancient Roman ship lies there after sinking in the 6th century AD while transporting prefabricated pieces of marble intended for an early church. The vehicles produced a detailed survey and detected other ships carrying columns made from the same material.

[04:33] AUDIO: Establishing an underwater internet for AUVs is difficult, however. Land-based Wi-Fi relies on electromagnetic waves which travel only a few centimetres through water. A more complicated combination of methods is therefore necessary. Light can carry data across short distances while acoustic waves are used over longer ones.

[04:59] AUDIO: Researchers are also testing more inventive arrangements. One vehicle working on the seabed can pass its data to another, which rises to the surface and sends the information to the team by satellite. A further system lets AUVs exchange seabed scans and related data. If one vehicle notices an unusual object, it can transmit the object's coordinates to a nearby AUV equipped with better cameras, so that the second machine can inspect it closely.

[05:34] AUDIO: Marine archeologists see enormous possibilities in this technology. One planned location for these vehicles is the Gulf of Berati, off Italy. A Roman vessel about 2,000 years old was found there in 1974, at a depth of 18 metres. It had been carrying medical supplies in containers made of wood or tin.

[05:59] AUDIO: The cargo reveals treatments used at the time, including tablets that were probably dissolved to make a liquid for washing the eyes. Other Roman ships sank close by with their loads and some contained enormous terracotta jars. Some of those jars transported olive oil while others carried wine. Often the containers are all that can still be seen because the wooden hulls lie buried beneath seabed silt.
[06:29] AUDIO: Another project that's about to... That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to...
